body:
Battery capacity, measured in milliamp hours, or mAh, is the number that product pages put in bold, and it is easy to assume that a bigger number always means a longer-lasting device. It is one factor, but it is not the whole story. How long a vape runs depends on how much energy the battery holds, how much energy each puff uses, how efficiently the device uses power and how you use it. This guide explains what mAh tells you, why power use matters, how puff counts relate to batteries, what real-world factors change battery life, how to read product pages, with a worked example you can follow, and how to look after a battery. It is written for adults aged 21 and over. Nicotine is addictive.

## What mAh tells you
mAh measures how much charge a battery holds. A 1,000 mAh battery holds twice the charge of a 500 mAh one, all else equal. It is like the size of a fuel tank. A bigger tank can go further, but how far depends on how thirsty the engine is. Capacity is usually quoted at the battery's nominal voltage, which for most lithium-ion cells is 3.7 volts.

## From mAh to energy
To compare batteries properly, it helps to turn mAh into watt-hours, which is a measure of energy. Multiply the capacity in amp hours by the voltage. A 1,000 mAh battery is 1 amp hour. At 3.7 volts, that is 3.7 watt-hours. A 500 mAh battery is 1.85 watt-hours. A 2,000 mAh battery is 7.4 watt-hours. Energy is what is actually spent when you puff.

## Power use matters
A device that runs at low power uses less energy per puff than a high-wattage one. Boost modes drain the battery faster. So a smaller battery on an efficient device can last as long as a bigger one on a power-hungry device. Energy per puff is power multiplied by time, so a 10-watt device taking a 2-second puff uses 20 joules, and a 25-watt device taking the same puff uses 50 joules, two and a half times as much.

### A worked example
Take a 1,000 mAh battery at 3.7 volts, which holds 3.7 watt-hours, or about 13,300 joules. At 10 watts for a 2-second puff, each puff uses about 20 joules, so the battery could in theory supply about 660 puffs. At 25 watts for a 3-second puff, each puff uses 75 joules, so you would get about 177 puffs. The same battery gives very different results, which shows why mAh alone does not predict battery life. Real results are lower, because of conversion losses and the battery not being fully drained, but the comparison holds.

## Puff counts and batteries
Puff counts on disposables are set mostly by liquid volume, with the battery sized to match. A larger liquid reservoir needs a larger battery to vaporize it all, so high puff counts and large batteries go together. See [puff counts explained](/blog/puff-count-explained/). Rechargeable models can add extra puffs by charging, which is why many large devices have USB-C ports. For a non-rechargeable device, the battery is sized to last about as long as the liquid, and whichever runs out first ends the device.

## Real-world factors
- **Draw length and frequency:** longer, more frequent draws use more energy.
- **Temperature:** batteries lose capacity when cold, and very high heat shortens their life.
- **Age:** capacity falls after many charge cycles. A battery that is a year old can hold noticeably less than when new.
- **Coil resistance:** lower resistance coils draw more current at the same voltage.
- **Power setting:** higher wattage uses more energy per second.
- **Standby drain:** some devices use a small amount of power when idle.

## Why bigger is not always better
A larger battery adds weight and size, takes longer to charge and may not suit a small device. Some small, efficient devices are designed around a modest battery and give long life. A large battery in a device that uses lots of power may still run out quickly. The sensible comparison is between devices of the same type and power level.

## Reading product pages
Look for mAh and for any mention of USB-C charging or pass-through. Check whether the battery is rechargeable and how long charging takes. If puff counts are listed, compare them with the battery size, because a very high puff count with a very small battery is a sign to read carefully. Our [rechargeable versus non-rechargeable article](/blog/rechargeable-vs-non-rechargeable-disposables/) shows what to check.

## Charging time
Charging time depends on the battery size and the charger. A rough guide is that a small battery charges in under an hour, and a large one in one to two hours. Using a reputable charger and a standard cable helps. See [how to charge a disposable](/blog/how-to-charge-a-disposable/).

## Looking after it
Care extends life. Avoid heat and cold, charge before the battery is fully empty when you can, unplug when full and do not leave a device charging unattended. See [battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/) and [extending battery life](/blog/how-to-extend-vape-battery-life/). A battery that is looked after can serve for many months.

## Signs of a wearing battery
- It drains faster than it used to.
- It takes longer to charge, or does not reach full.
- It feels warm when idle.
- The device shuts off with charge remaining.

If you see these signs, retire the device, and dispose of it properly.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Does a higher mAh mean more puffs?
Generally more energy, but puff counts depend on liquid and power too. Compare devices of the same type.

### Can I replace the battery in a disposable?
No. Disposable batteries are sealed. Do not try to open the device.

### Why does my device run out faster in winter?
Cold reduces battery capacity temporarily. Keep the device warm in an inside pocket, and let it warm to room temperature before charging.

### Is it a problem to charge a half-empty battery?
No. Partial top-ups are fine, and often better for a battery than running it to empty.

### What does pass-through mean?
It means that the device can be used while charging. It is convenient, but using a device while it charges makes it warmer, so do it sparingly.

## Shop
Browse [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/) and [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Comparing two devices with numbers
Device A is a pod kit with a 500 mAh battery, a 1.0 ohm coil and a fixed 12 watts. Device B is a pod kit with a 1,000 mAh battery, a 0.6 ohm coil and a fixed 25 watts. Device A holds 1.85 watt-hours, about 6,660 joules, and uses about 24 joules for a 2-second puff, so in theory it supplies about 277 puffs. Device B holds 3.7 watt-hours, about 13,320 joules, and uses about 50 joules for a 2-second puff, so it supplies about 266 puffs. The second battery is twice the size, but because the device uses more than twice the power, it gives about the same number of puffs. The size of the battery alone would have misled you.

## What to look for when you shop
- **mAh and watts together,** not either on its own.
- **Whether the battery can be recharged,** and how.
- **Reviews of real-world battery life** from users with a similar style.
- **Charging speed,** especially for large batteries.
- **Battery protections,** such as overheating and short-circuit protection.

## Charging habits that help
Charge when you notice the battery getting low, instead of letting it hit zero. Use a reputable charger. Unplug when full. Avoid charging in heat or direct sun. If you will not use a device for a while, store it partly charged. These habits slow the natural loss of capacity and keep the battery in good shape.

## What changes as a battery ages
A new battery delivers its full rated capacity. After a few hundred charge cycles, it may hold 80 percent or less. You will notice shorter life between charges, and possibly slower charging. That is normal, and it is the reason batteries are consumables. When a device no longer lasts as long as you need, it is time to replace it, and to dispose of the old one responsibly. See [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/).

## How disposables hide the maths
In a disposable, the maker matches battery, coil and liquid, so that the puff count is a reasonable estimate. You do not have to do any calculation. The numbers matter when you compare devices: a 50,000-puff device needs far more energy than a 5,000-puff device, and the battery and liquid are sized accordingly. If you see a very high puff count with a very small battery listed, read carefully, and compare it with similar devices.

### Frequently asked questions about batteries and puffs
**Why does a device with a screen drain faster?** The screen and electronics use a small amount of power, so devices with displays can run through a battery a little faster.

**Does a bigger battery take longer to charge?** Yes, usually, unless the charger and device support faster charging. Allow more time for larger batteries.

**Can I use a power bank to charge?** Yes, with a standard cable, as long as the power bank is reputable and the device accepts it. Avoid leaving it charging unattended.

faq.a: Milliamp hours, a measure of how much charge a battery holds. Higher means a larger charge, all else equal.

faq.q: Does more mAh always mean longer battery life?
faq.a: No. Power use matters as much. A device at higher wattage uses more energy per puff.

faq.q: How can I compare batteries properly?
faq.a: Convert mAh to watt-hours by multiplying amp hours by the voltage, about 3.7 volts for most lithium-ion cells.

faq.q: How do puff counts relate to batteries?
faq.a: Puff counts are set mostly by liquid volume, with the battery sized to match. Rechargeable models can add extra puffs by charging.

faq.q: Why does cold weather shorten battery life?
faq.a: Batteries lose capacity when cold. The effect is temporary and reverses as the battery warms.

faq.q: How can I make a battery last?
faq.a: Avoid heat and cold, charge before it is fully empty when you can, unplug when full and use a suitable charger.
